Water is central to our people, our economies, and our sustainable development ambitions. It supports public health, agriculture, tourism, food security, and resilience in the face of climate change. For St. Kitts and Nevis, which unlike Jamaica is one of the most water-scarce countries in the world, securing reliable and sustainable water supplies has become one of our highest national priorities. Like many island nations, we are experiencing increasing rainfall variability, prolonged drought conditions, declining groundwater recharge, and growing pressure on traditional water sources. In terms of technical considerations, our experience demonstrates that water security requires solutions tailored to the specific circumstances of each island. St. Kitts and Nevis has historically depended heavily on groundwater and surface water sources. Climate change has increased the vulnerability of these sources. reinforcing the need for greater diversification and resilience. Over the past several years, we have made significant investments to strengthen national water supply. In 2026, we commissioned the Bastia Desalination Plant, a 2 million gallon per day desalination facility valued at EC$50 million. This project has transformed water security for Bastia, and surrounding communities by providing a reliable, continuous source of water. Additional investments have included the integration of the Cayonne Well into the national system, the commissioning of the Canada Estate Desalination Plant, and continued groundwater exploration. These investments have increased national production capacity to 8 million gallons per day, exceeding current demand. Although we acknowledge that 24-hour water access is not uniform across all communities, so that's still a work in progress. Our supply profile has also become more balanced. Approximately 52% of national supply comes from groundwater, 22% from surface water, and and 26% from desalination. This diversification strengthens our ability to manage drought conditions and climate-related disruptions. The next phase of our transformation focuses on improving efficiency and strengthening the systems that deliver water to our communities through the TransWater project, which we expect to be approved by the Green Climate Fund in 2027. We are advancing investments in water resource monitoring, storage capacity, and like the minister from Jamaica said, heavily towards digitalization in terms of smart metering, SCADA systems, utility management, and non-water— non-revenue water reduction. We also have an incredibly high NRW rate of about 50%.

non-revenue water.

Reducing water losses is a critical priority. In terms of financial considerations, water security requires sustained investment. SIDS face unique challenges including high infrastructure costs, limited economies of scale, and significant maintenance requirements. An important component of sustainable water financing is tariff reform. As water systems become more resilient and investments increase, pricing structures must evolve support long-term operation and maintenance while ensuring affordability for vulnerable households. Willing— willingness to pay surveys that we have conducted provide value— valuable evidence to guide this process. The findings show that willingness to pay is closely connected to affordability, perceptions of fairness, trust, and and visible improvements in service delivery. While approximately 95% of households report having piped water to their homes, only about 24% indicate some willingness to pay for reliable improvements, and this support was dependent on confidence that these improvements would be delivered. In Nevis, willingness to pay was approximate approximately 6%, reflecting perception that existing water costs are already high. So we have a big discrepancy in the cost of water across both islands, St. Kitts and Nevis, with Nevis paying much higher rates for water. Tariff reform must therefore be approached as part of a broader social partnership. Consumers must understand how revenue supports Reliable services, conservation, infrastructure maintenance, and climate resilience. In terms of regulatory and institutional considerations, effective water management requires coordination across government sectors. Finally, in terms of social considerations, Water security is ultimately about people. Infrastructure and technology must be supported by public understanding, community participation, and trust. The TransWater project, which we hope to be approved, places strong emphasis on water literacy, behavior change, tariff awareness, and community partnerships. The willingness to pay surveys The findings reinforce the importance of sustained communication. Older persons, persons with disabilities, and vulnerable households may face additional challenges during periods of water stress. Inclusive planning and accessible support mechanisms are therefore essential components of a resilient water sector. In conclusion, the experience of St. Kitts and Nevis demonstrates that meaningful progress in water security is achievable through vision, partnership, and sustained commitment. We are building a water sector supported by diversified sources, stronger infrastructure, improved governance, modern technology, sustainable financing, and improve communities. We have reached a very good quality of the water according to standards, and we managed also to increase through better quality the amount of water sales. In fact, more than 2 million plastic bottles were saved last year. We are also now using the experience we gained in desalination and membrane technology to treat wastewater. As mentioned earlier, we now are treating wastewater through RO membranes. We have a multi-stage process whereby secondary class water is processed through ultrafiltration membranes and advanced oxidation. Producing Class A reclaimed water. Class A reclaimed water is water that can be irrigated to crops that can be eaten raw. So this is the highest standard of water that can be produced. We are now also— we also now have a dedicated network for secondary water which uses and distributes water through through intelligent smart dispensers based on cropless. We now have more than 1,500 farmers benefiting from this new source. Of course, we do hope that less water is abstracted from groundwater so that the natural water table will recharge over the next years. So conservation. Initially, the price of water in Malta was quite low, and as one of the laws of economics suggests, if the price is low, then the demand will be quite high because obviously it's more affordable. So we decided to penalize those who consume water irresponsibly. In Malta, we have a 2-tier system whereby the first 33 cubic meters of water consumed by each individual, there is a tariff for it. It's around €1.60. But if that value is exceeded, then the cost, the price will go up to €5. exceeding €5. Okay, um, we do have an issue with, of course, tourism, but we are lucky most of the hotels are located on the shoreline. So, um, we started promoting, um, desalination also on-site production of water in the major hotels. In fact, we do give this service to these hotels. We design and build systems for them and operate them on their behalf, obviously at a cost. And this obviously helped to reduce the peak, especially in summer. So how did we create this self-sustaining utility? Of course, phase 1 was eradicating the losses, reducing the losses. By investing in the network and investing in smart metering. This helped us secure more cash and increase the revenue, which in turn helped us to reinvest in our operation. We are now at a point whereby we are also looking at maximizing on our operation. Also valorizing waste streams. We're looking at valorizing especially the brine stream. Brine is the reject coming out of the RO plant, which is around 60% of what goes in. Okay. We are looking at producing hydrogen from brine, looking at producing magnesium from brine. And also producing chemicals which can be used internally for remineralization. As you may know, desalination removes all minerals from seawater. So we are piloting a system whereby the brine gives us back the minerals to put in the water before it is distributed. So lessons learned: you cannot sell what you lose, you cannot manage what you cannot measure. Okay, so this is very important. Um, quality shifts the markets. We have seen an improvement in the water quality supply to the consumers. This has increased the consumption, obviously yielding more revenue to the corporation. In turn, we can invest more and obviously benefiting also from the single-use plastic waste and of course the circular economy. Every drop here has dual utility. So we produce water, we distribute wastewater, water, would collect wastewater, and that water is then reused for agricultural purposes. So it's very important also to focus on the wastewater network so as to collect, you know, the water consumed by the general public. Thank you.

Thank you, Ing-Sacko, for sharing some of Malta's lessons learned and best practices through your water crisis, and also for outlining for us very comprehensively Malta's water strategy. I would now like to invite our final speaker for this session, Ms. Asha Challenger from the Permanent Mission of Antigua and Barbuda, one of our esteemed co-organizers. Thank you, Ms. of course, to take the floor.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and greetings to Mr. Samuda. Thank you for joining us, Madam UNEP DSG Marima, Ambassador Mellie, distinguished colleagues. Thank you for this opportunity to present Antigua and Barbuda's perspective on this critically important issue of sustainable sustainable water use. The colleagues from the Antigua Public Utilities Authority, our national water management agency, weren't able to attend today, so I will share some remarks on behalf of the authority. Antigua and Barbuda, like many small island developing states, faces structural constraints in securing sustainable water resources. As mentioned before, limited natural freshwater availability Groundwater salinization in low-lying coastal areas, and the logistical challenges of supplying water across dispersed communities create persistent vulnerabilities. These challenges are compounded by climate change, including prolonged droughts, increasingly variable rainfall, and growing water demand from key sectors such as agriculture and tourism. To address these challenges, Antigua and Barbuda has made substantial investments in modernizing its water infrastructure despite the significant financial burden. The, the authority has been systematically replacing aging transmission lines with high-density polyethylene pipelines, improving network efficiency reducing leakage, and strengthening the resilience of the national water distribution system. Climate change has also had a profound impact on the country's surface water resources. Historically, reservoirs provided up to 9 months of water production annually. Today, that period has declined to between 3 to 5 months, with some years experiencing complete depletion due to prolonged droughts, increased evaporation, and increasingly erratic rainfall. As a result, desalination has become an indispensable component of the national water supply. While it provides a reliable source of fresh water, it is significantly more expensive than surface water and groundwater because of its high energy consumption and operational This growing reliance underscores the importance of integrated water management— integrated water resources management to diversify water sources, improve efficiency, and build long-term climate resilience. Antigua and Barbuda is therefore pleased to participate in this side event to highlight national progress, share lessons learned through technical cooperation with the Republic of Malta, and to identify priority actions to strengthen water resilience in support of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS. So, as said before, Antigua and Barbuda's water sector faces a range of interconnected challenges common to many SIDS. Heavy reliance on desalination ensures a dependable water supply but entails significant energy costs. At the same time, aging transmission and distribution infrastructure contributes to high levels of non-revenue water, which fluctuates between 45% and 65%. Climate change has also undermined water security through saltwater intrusion, which has significantly reduced groundwater production and forced 3 well fields, particularly within the country's highly productive but vulnerable karstic aquifers offline for extended periods. Together with declining surface water availability, these pressures have increased dependence on desalination and reinforced the need for an integrated, climate-resilient approach to water resource management. In this context, reducing non-revenue water is not simply a technical objective, it is an economic imperative. I will now shift to talking more about technical cooperation. Since 2022, Antigua and Barbuda and Malta commenced technical cooperation. In November of that year, a team of 5 technicians traveled to Malta to see firsthand the gains that a similar island country has made through innovative processes to improve their water distribution and reduce non-revenue water. The team learned that Antigua and Barbuda's present challenges were very similar challenges that Malta faced— had to face and have since overcome. This presented an opportunity to learn practices and methods from Malta. This partnership is already producing tangible results. In 2025, Antigua and Barbuda undertook undertook a second technical mission to Malta focused on reducing water losses and improving the efficiency of the water distribution system. Our engineers worked alongside with experts from the Energy and Water Agency and the Water Services Corporation to strengthen our capacity in areas such as leakage detection, pressure management, and network optimization. Beyond technical knowledge exchange, The partnership has also created practical opportunities for cooperation, including support with procurement processes and collaboration on digital mapping of our water network. We see this as an excellent example of how partnerships can deliver practical, cost-effective solutions and strengthen water security and advance the implementation of ABAS for SIDS. This cooperation has reinforced several important lessons that are relevant across many other SIDS. We have seen that effective leakage management is one of the most impactful and cost-effective ways to improve water security, while continuous data monitoring and pressure management and GIS-based network mapping are essential for optimizing water water distribution systems. We have also learned that partnerships on procurement can help small island utilities reduce costs and improve access to critical equipment and technologies. These lessons are directly informing Antigua and Barbuda's national priorities. We are now focused on expanding pressure management zones and installing pressure reducing valves, improving metering and adopting new metering technologies, strengthening our hydrological and operational data systems, and reducing non-revenue water through targeted infrastructure upgrades. These investments will help us build a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable water sector while ensuring that our limited water resources are managed as effectively as possible. In conclusion, we call on further collaborations and the international community to continue to support SIDS in scaling integrated water management resources, continue strengthening bilateral and multilateral partnerships that can deliver tangible technical benefits, and finally, expand access to climate finance for water system resilience. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Challenger, for your comprehensive intervention, and of course to all of our speakers, many focusing on the importance of partnerships, investments, financing, as well as on getting the regulation, policy, and governance-related issues right. We will now move on to our final session, and we'll invite— we will invite our respondents to add additional national perspectives as well as to look ahead. In that context, I would ask the respondents to provide their perspectives as concisely as possible, please, on what is the current landscape for bilateral, regional, and international partnerships for SIDS on sustainable water management, and what are the current gaps for the implementation of ABAS in the context of sustainable water management. Now I would like to give the floor to our first speaker, Ms. Rhoda Roko Tui-Bau. I hope I pronounced that correctly. From the Permanent Mission of Fiji, who is also one of our co-organizers, so thank you very much for that. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair, Honorable Minister, distinguished Excellencies and representatives. Allow me to thank Malta, Antigua and Barbuda, Thank you, OHRLLS, for convening us this afternoon. Also, to our fellow panelists for their valuable insights. For Fiji and many Pacific Small Island Developing States, water security is climate security. This challenge is not one of water availability alone, but of ensuring reliable, safe, and climate-resilient access to water across geographically dispersed islands and vulnerable coastal communities. I will speak on 3 of Fiji's national experiences. One on governance. Fiji's transition from a fragmented infrastructure-focused approach towards an integrated water resource management has allowed endorsement of a national resource management and sanitation policy which sets our strategic direction. Our new integrated water resource management plan that has provided practical vision action across water, sanitation, agriculture, health, and disaster risk management. Second, on efficiency, close to half of the water we extract is some way 49% and is lost in distribution that reaches households. For small island states, reducing these losses can drive— can deliver more water quickly and more affordably rather than building new dams and desalination plants. Managing what we already have in itself is an adaptation strategy. And third, partnerships and people. We are grounded in traditional stewardships, women's leadership, and locally led adaptation with the support of Australian partnerships while looking to the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund, as well as regional partners, to finance resilient infrastructure. Yet these mechanisms remain slow and are limited to capacity and disproportionately burdensome. This then brings me to the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Seeds, ABUS, that's rightly called for the support for integrated water management. Therefore, the gap is of implementation, which turns commitments into predictable and accessible finance, targeted technology transfer, and sustainable capacity building to enable reaching our community level and sustainably the ultimately determined. I conclude in saying Fiji stands ready to work with all partners to close this gap and to turn water insecurity into shared opportunity, a water-resilient future, and an achievement towards SDG 6.

Thank you. Thank you very much, Ms. Roko Tuibau, for your perspectives from Fiji. Our next speaker is Ms. Jocelyn Kroes, Director of Department of Foreign Affairs of Aruba. Jocelyn, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair.

As a small island with extremely limited natural freshwater resources, Aruba's experience demonstrates that sustainable water management requires long-term vision, innovation, and enduring partnerships. Aruba has relied on seawater desalination for nearly a century, making it one of the pioneers in large-scale desalination. The nation among small island states. Over the decades, continuous investments in technology, infrastructure, and human capital has allowed us to provide safe and reliable drinking water while adapting to growing demands, climate variability, and the needs of a highly tourism-dependent economy. We have worked with many, many actors along the way. Our approach is guided by the RAS framework: reliability, affordability, and sustainability. Reliability means for us ensuring uninterrupted access to safe drinking water. Affordability ensures services remain accessible while financially viable. And sustainability drives investments in efficiency, water reuse, and environmental stewardship for future generations. Yes, partnerships have been central to this success. We are bound by a common ocean in the region, and thus at this level we benefit from cooperation through UNEP's Caribbean Environmental Program, including the PROCARIBE+ Ocean Coordination Mechanism, UNESCO's IOC, IHP, and MAB programs, the Association of Caribbean States, AEOSIS, regional universities, and bilateral partnerships. These collaborations support integrated water resource management, ocean governance, climate resilience, scientific cooperation, and sustainable development. This approach, strengthened by Aruba's recent designation as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, has led to an international recognition of areas that seek to reconcile biodiversity Conservation. Conservation with sustainable development by integrating environmental protection, scientific research, education, and community, community participation, and recognizes the interconnectedness of our terrestrial, coastal, and marine ecosystems and provides a framework for managing them in integrated manners. It also offers an opportunity for Aruba to serve as a living laboratory where ecosystem-based and nature-based solutions can be tested and shared, strengthening water security, climate resilience, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable tourism. It is this way that a biosphere reserve supports integrated approach for our water management as espoused in the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS. We also rely on data for informed decision-making, and like one of the key challenges identified in the implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS is indeed strengthening capacity to collect and manage and share long-term environmental data, we are also in our case, very much challenged in this area. Finally, Aruba wishes to emphasize that while short-term project partnerships may often be the norm in larger countries, SIDS benefit most from long-term partnerships built on trust, continuity, and institutional memory. Water security is a long-term endeavor that requires sustained investment, knowledge sharing, capacity building, and collaboration. Aruba stands ready to continue working with fellow SIDS and partners to transform water scarcity into lasting water security and resilience.

I thank you. Thank you very much, Ms. Cruz, for offering Aruba's perspectives. And now our final speaker for Our next speaker for this session is Mr. Ho Chian Kai from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Singapore. Mr. Ho, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair. My thanks also to the distinguished panelists for their very informative presentations on the challenges and approaches to water management. Allow me to say a few brief words from Singapore's perspective. As a small and densely populated island city-state with limited natural resources, Singapore is among the world's most water-stressed countries. Despite this, decades of long-term planning by PUB, our national water agency, have given us a diversified water portfolio that positions us to adapt to the challenges of climate change while ensuring universal and predictable access to water. We have progressively expanded our water sources beyond rainwater to include climate-resilient alternatives such as recycled and desalinated water, while consistently treating conservation as a core pillar of water security. But sustainable water management requires more than just a one-time investment. It needs continuous financing and innovation. Just last month, we committed close to $100 million in research funding to advance municipal and industrial water solutions. This year will also mark the completion of Phase 2 of our deep tunnel sewerage system, which will enable large-scale recycling of used water for decades to come. Singapore's approach has been underpinned by sustained efforts to secure public buy-in on treating water use responsibly and efficiently. Community education initiatives to build trust in our water management system systems, together with consistent water conservation messaging, have instilled in our people a strong sense of the necessity of sustainable water practices. But of course, no country can achieve sustainable water management alone. Singapore has drawn on international partnerships to address challenges posed by population growth and the impact of climate change. We have shared our experiences and best practices through capacity-building programmes, for fellow developing countries and are proud to host the flagship biennial Singapore International Water Week to create an open marketplace for knowledge, technology, capacity building, and partnerships between governments, businesses, academia, and civil society. I thank you.

Thank you very much. Unfortunately, we will not have enough time for an open discussion, but I would like to thank all of our speakers for providing such rich interventions, which will definitely inform our collective efforts going forward towards effective water management in SIDS and Small Island States. And with that, I would like to give the floor to Ambassador Natasha Melly, Permanent Representative of Malta, for closing remarks and to give us some reflections on the way forward, and of course to close our meeting. Thank you very much.

Thank you.
